_: beginner-pinyin.json — the table behind decks/Mandarin-Pinyin-and-Tones.folio-deck.json, read by build-beginner.js. Every IPA value and every sentence in `like`, `says` and `rule` is taken from the two Wikipedia articles named in `sources` at the revisions given (CC BY-SA 4.0); wiki markup is turned into <b> and <i>, a cut inside a passage is marked […], a cross-reference to another section ('see below', 'see syllabic fricatives') and a Taiwanese variant are dropped, and nothing is reworded. `cls` is the row's place and manner in the Pinyin article's own consonant table. The article's description column also calls f, s, x and sh 'aspirated'; that word is not carried, the same article's consonant table listing them as plain fricatives. Example words are NOT in this file: the builder takes them from the shipped Level 1 to 3 decks, so each has the deck's own reading, meaning and speaker. A row's `key` is what mandarin-ids.json pins its card id to — never rename one.

tones.name: first tone
tones.says: First tone is a high-level tone. It is a steady high sound, produced as if it were being sung instead of spoken.

tones.name: second tone
tones.says: Second tone is a rising tone. It is usually described as a high-rising (35), with the sound that rises from middle to high pitch (like in the English "What?!").

tones.name: third tone
tones.says: Third tone is a low tone. It is also often termed a "dipping tone". This tone is often demonstrated as having a rise in pitch after the low fall; […] When a third-tone syllable is not said in isolation, this rise is normally heard only if it appears at the end of a sentence or before a pause, and then usually only on stressed monosyllables.

tones.name: fourth tone
tones.says: Fourth tone is a falling tone. It features a sharp fall from high to lower pitch (as is heard in curt commands in English, such as "Stop!").

tones.name: neutral tone
tones.says: Also called fifth tone or zeroth tone […], the neutral tone is sometimes thought of as a lack of tone. It is associated with weak syllables, which are generally somewhat shorter than tonic syllables. […] The pitch of a syllable with neutral tone is determined by the tone of the preceding syllable.

rules.name: where the tone mark goes
rules.rule: If there is an a or an e, it will take the tone mark. In the combination ou, then the o takes the tone mark. Otherwise, the second vowel takes the tone mark.

rules.name: two third tones together
rules.rule: When there are two consecutive third-tone syllables, the first of them is pronounced with second tone.
rules.also: Tone sandhi is not ordinarily reflected in pinyin spelling.

rules.name: the tone of 不
rules.rule: 不 is pronounced with second tone when followed by a fourth tone syllable. In other cases, 不 is pronounced with fourth tone.
rules.house: The Level 1 deck writes this change: bú before a fourth tone.

rules.name: the tone of 一
rules.rule: 一 is pronounced with second tone when followed by a fourth tone syllable. Before a first, second or third tone syllable, 一 is pronounced with fourth tone. When final, or when it comes at the end of a multi-syllable word (regardless of the first tone of the next word), 一 is pronounced with first tone.
rules.house: The Level 1 deck writes this change: yí before a fourth tone, yì before the others.

initials.note: Y, w, and yu are equivalent to the semivowel medials i, u, and ü. They are spelled differently when there is no initial consonant in order to mark a new syllable. […] In addition, y and w are added to fully vocalic i, u, and ü when these occur without an initial consonant, so that they are written yi, wu, and yu.

finals.after: after z, c, s, zh, ch, sh, r
finals.like: -i is a buzzed continuation of the consonant following z-, c-, s-, zh-, ch-, sh- or r-. In all other cases, -i has the sound of bee.
